subject: Career
title: Reframing Experience for a New Field
description: A short lesson to help you apply Reframing Experience for a New Field.

hook.text: 'I managed a $2M restaurant budget' becomes 'I managed a $2M P&L.' Same fact, different industry language.

buildup.text: Every industry has its own vocabulary. Translating your experience into the new field's language is essential.

discovery.text: The skill is the same. The framing makes it relevant. 'Teaching' becomes 'training.' 'Selling' becomes 'business development.'

twist.text: Hiring managers often can't see cross-industry parallels. Your job is to draw the connection for them.

climax.text: Study job descriptions in your target field. Map your experience to their exact keywords.

punchline.text: Same skills, new language. Translation is the strategy.

quiz.question: Why is reframing experience important in career transitions?
options: Hiring managers can't always see cross-industry parallels

details.summary: Reframing translates your past accomplishments into the language and priorities of your target industry. The same skill described differently can either sound irrelevant or instantly compelling to a new employer.
details.whyItMatters: Without reframing, career changers appear unqualified on paper despite holding deeply relevant capabilities. Language bridges the perception gap.
takeaways: Study job descriptions in your target field to learn its vocabulary
Map your achievements to the outcome metrics the new field values
Practice your reframed narrative until it feels natural

faq.question: How do you learn the vocabulary of an entirely new industry?
faq.answer: Read fifty job descriptions in the target field, follow industry thought leaders, and attend webinars or meetups. Within a few weeks you will absorb the jargon and be able to describe your experience using language insiders recognize.

faq.question: Is reframing the same as exaggerating or misrepresenting experience?
faq.answer: Not at all. Reframing presents truthful accomplishments in contextually relevant language. Exaggerating invents or inflates results. If you managed a team of ten and call it people leadership, that is reframing. Calling it executive leadership is exaggeration.
